item.title: Emulating spatially extended systems using Fourier Neural Operator
item.description: arXiv:2611.18007v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Operator Learning (OL) algorithms approximate underlying mathematical operators by mapping entire classes of input functions to their corresponding solutions. For instance, architectures such as the Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) have been trained on numerical datasets generated by isolated, stiff ionic models to provide a data-driven alternative to traditional numerical integration schemes. However, real-world biological and physical systems typically consist of interconnected spatial units arranged in complex, heterogeneous networks. Motivated by this observation, we generalize this data-driven framework to spatially extended systems defined on diverse graph topologies, ranging from Erdos-Renyi to Barabasi-Albert networks. Furthermore, we evaluate the proposed approach on empirical data, demonstrating its ability to accurately and efficiently model task-oriented neural activity.
item.dc:creator: Gabriele Poccianti, Duccio Fanelli

item.title: Latent resonances in oscillator networks
item.description: arXiv:2611.18031v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In networks of coupled oscillators, from neural circuits to power grids, damping is expected to suppress oscillations because of its dissipativity. Here we show that local damping can, counterintuitively, amplify oscillations along some input-output channels, while the network's global oscillation energy decreases and its spectral properties improve. The amplified oscillation arises from a latent resonance that lies in the spectrum yet barely manifests. The added passive damping reshapes this resonance by mixing it with adjacent eigenmodes. In random power-grid networks, damping can boost weakly responding channels by more than an order of magnitude, while subdominant channels can grow to exceed the originally strongest channel. Damping thus not only suppresses oscillations but also provides a way to redistribute oscillatory energy. For any passive network, the amplified response and its upper bound follow exactly from baseline quantities, offering a principled route for network design and control.
item.dc:creator: Junjie Xiao, Renaud Lambiotte, Hiroshi Kori

item.title: Switching between Collective Network Dynamics driven by Time-Delay Plasticity
item.description: arXiv:2605.23520v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We show that time-delay plasticity provides a mechanism for switching between collective states in delay-coupled oscillator networks. In particular, we consider adaptive axonal delays (AADs), motivated by activity-dependent myelination in the brain, and demonstrate that AADs drive the network slowly along branches of phase-locked states until these lose transverse stability, producing explosive relaxation oscillations between collective states. We establish the mechanism for a ring network with an explicitly averageable adaptation rule, and show that a phenomenological myelination rule on human connectome data produces the same slow--fast scenario, together with frequency selection and the selection of chimera states.
item.dc:creator: Stefan Ruschel, Emanuil Hristov, Hil G. E. Meijer, Stephen Coombes, Rachel Nicks

item.title: Dynamical confinement creates quasi-critical scale-free dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2602.00374v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Scale-free avalanches are commonly interpreted as signatures of criticality. Conventional theoretical frameworks predict robust avalanche-size exponents $\tau$ bounded by $3/2$, while dissipation is expected to drive systems away from criticality, by progressively suppressing large events. Yet earthquakes and numerous dissipative experiments exhibit scale-free dynamics with non-universal exponents $\tau > 3/2$, challenging both expectations. Using the Olami-Feder-Christensen model as a minimal theoretical framework, we identify two fundamentally distinct routes to scale-free dynamics:a genuinely critical scenario, in which avalanches continuously explore the entire system and remain permanently capable of spanning it; and a quasi-critical scenario, in which dissipation and the traces left by past avalanches generate dynamical confinement. Rather than remaining at a critical point, the system explores a power-law distribution of distances to criticality. We show, using a simple analytical model, how this mechanism produces scale-free avalanche statistics with dissipation-dependent exponents exceeding $\tau = 3/2$. Our results establish a physical mechanism for scale-free dynamics beyond conventional criticality, providing a framework for understanding the non-universal avalanche statistics observed in earthquakes and dissipative systems.
item.dc:creator: K. Duplat, A. Douin, F. Detcheverry, O. Ramos
